---
title: "Cities, Infrastructure, and Urban Life（城市、基础设施与城市生活）"
---

## Urbanisation and Population Concentration（城市化与人口集中）

Urbanisation（城市化）is the process by which increasing proportions of a population move from rural areas（农村地区）to cities and urban settlements（城市和城市定居点）. In 1800, only about 3 percent of the world's population lived in cities. Today, more than 55 percent live in urban areas, and the United Nations projects（联合国预测）that this proportion will reach approximately 68 percent by 2050. Urbanisation is one of the most significant demographic transformations（人口转变）in human history, reshaping where people live, how they work, what they consume, and how they interact with each other and the natural environment.

People move to cities because cities offer concentrated economic opportunities（集中的经济机会）— more jobs, higher wages, greater diversity of employment, and more pathways for career advancement（职业发展路径）. Cities also offer better access to education（教育）, healthcare（医疗保健）, entertainment（娱乐）, cultural institutions（文化机构）, and social services（社会服务）. The concentration of people, businesses, and institutions in cities creates agglomeration economies（集聚经济）— the economic benefits that arise from proximity（邻近性）to other economic actors. Firms located near suppliers（供应商）, customers（客户）, competitors（竞争者）, and a deep labour market（深厚的劳动市场）benefit from lower transaction costs（更低的交易成本）, faster knowledge exchange（更快的知识交流）, and access to specialised services（专业化服务）that would not be viable in smaller, more dispersed settlements.

Population concentration（人口集中）in cities creates both opportunities and challenges that scale with density（随密度变化）. Density allows efficient provision of public services（公共服务的高效供给）— public transport（公共交通）, water supply（供水）, electricity（电力）, waste collection（垃圾收集）— because infrastructure serves more people per unit of investment in dense areas than in dispersed rural settlements. Density enables the exchange of ideas and knowledge（思想和知识交流）, driving innovation（创新）through the interaction of diverse people with different skills, perspectives, and expertise. Density supports a rich cultural and social life（丰富的文化和社会生活）with diverse options for dining, entertainment, arts, and social interaction that smaller settlements cannot sustain.

Rapid urbanisation（快速城市化）can outpace the development of infrastructure, services, and governance capacity（治理能力）. When too many people move to a city too quickly, housing becomes scarce and expensive（住房稀缺且昂贵）, transport systems become overcrowded（过度拥挤）, water and sanitation systems（供水和卫生系统）are overwhelmed, and pollution（污染）increases. Informal settlements（非正式定居点）or slums（贫民窟）develop when the formal housing market（正式住房市场）cannot meet demand from low-income migrants（低收入移民）. These settlements often lack basic services — clean water, sewage disposal（污水处理）, electricity, paved roads（铺装道路）— and expose residents to health hazards（健康危害）, environmental risks（环境风险）, and tenure insecurity（居住权不安全）.

The rate and pattern of urbanisation vary greatly between regions and stages of development. In many developing countries（发展中国家）, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa（撒哈拉以南非洲）and South Asia（南亚）, urbanisation is happening very rapidly, creating enormous pressure on urban infrastructure and governance. In developed countries（发达国家）, urbanisation has largely stabilised（基本稳定）at high levels, and the focus has shifted from managing growth to improving the quality of urban life — reducing inequality（减少不平等）, improving sustainability（提高可持续性）, upgrading aging infrastructure（升级老化基础设施）, and addressing the social isolation（社会隔离）and affordability crises（可负担性危机）that characterise many mature cities.

Urbanisation therefore functions as the mechanism through which populations concentrate in cities and how this concentration creates both economic opportunities and urban challenges. The vocabulary of urbanisation — urbanisation, agglomeration economy, population concentration, rapid urbanisation, informal settlement — names the processes through which people move to cities and the conditions that determine whether urbanisation produces economic growth or urban crisis. Urban texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from rural-to-urban migration through population concentration to the urban outcomes that determine whether cities become engines of prosperity or centres of inequality and environmental degradation.

## Population Density and Urban Pressure（人口密度与城市压力）

Population density（人口密度）measures the number of people living in a given area, usually expressed as persons per square kilometre（每平方公里人数）. High population density is a defining characteristic of cities and affects almost every aspect of urban life — how people move, where they live, what services are available, how the environment is affected, and how social interactions occur. Density is not inherently good or bad; its effects depend on how well the city is planned, managed, and equipped to serve its concentrated population.

High density creates pressure on urban systems（城市系统压力）when infrastructure and services do not scale proportionally（成比例地）with population growth. Transport systems must move large numbers of people efficiently between residential areas（居住区）, employment centres（就业中心）, schools, and services. Housing must accommodate many people in limited space while maintaining acceptable living standards（可接受的生活标准）. Water, electricity, and waste systems must serve concentrated demand without breakdown or degradation of service quality. When density is very high and infrastructure is inadequate, these systems become strained（紧张）, producing congestion, shortages, and declining quality of life.

Urban pressure（城市压力）manifests in several visible forms. Traffic congestion（交通拥堵）wastes time and fuel, increases air pollution（空气污染）, reduces economic productivity, and diminishes quality of life. Housing affordability（住房可负担性）becomes a crisis when demand for housing in desirable locations far exceeds supply, driving prices and rents beyond what moderate-income households（中等收入家庭）can afford. Competition for space（空间竞争）pushes lower-income residents to peripheral areas（边缘地区）where transport costs are higher, services are fewer, and access to employment is more difficult — a spatial mismatch（空间错配）that reinforces economic inequality. Noise pollution（噪音污染）, reduced privacy（隐私减少）, and limited access to green space（绿地）affect mental health and wellbeing.

Density also affects social dynamics（社会动态）in complex ways. High density can increase social interaction（社会互动）, cultural diversity（文化多样性）, and the vibrancy（活力）of urban life. It can also increase stress（压力）, crime（犯罪）, and social conflict（社会冲突）when not managed through effective governance（有效治理）, adequate public services, and well-designed public spaces（设计良好的公共空间）. The design of urban spaces — parks（公园）, public squares（公共广场）, pedestrian areas（步行区）, community centres（社区中心）— can mitigate negative effects by providing spaces for recreation, social interaction, and community building（社区建设）that relieve the pressures of dense living.

Different cities manage density through different approaches that reflect their geography, history, culture, and governance. Tokyo（东京）and Hong Kong（香港）achieve very high density with efficient public transport, compact housing（紧凑型住房）, and mixed-use development（混合用途开发）that keeps daily destinations accessible. Many American cities（美国城市）have lower density with extensive car-dependent suburbs（依赖汽车的郊区）, producing longer commutes, higher per-capita emissions（更高的人均排放）, and greater infrastructure costs per resident. European cities（欧洲城市）often combine moderate density（中等密度）with strong public transport, cycling infrastructure（自行车基础设施）, and preserved public spaces. Each approach involves trade-offs between space, cost, transport efficiency, environmental impact, and quality of life.

Population density and urban pressure therefore represent the mechanism through which the concentration of people in limited space creates both the efficiencies that make cities productive and the pressures that make them challenging to manage. The vocabulary of density — population density, urban pressure, traffic congestion, housing affordability, spatial mismatch, social dynamic — names the conditions that arise when large numbers of people share limited urban space and the policy choices that determine whether density produces vibrant communities or overwhelmed systems. Urban texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from population concentration through infrastructure capacity to the urban outcomes that determine whether cities can serve their residents effectively or whether urban pressure degrades quality of life.

## Housing, Land, and Living Costs（住房、土地与生活成本）

Housing（住房）is one of the most basic human needs（基本人类需求）and typically the largest single expense（最大单项支出）for urban households. The cost of housing is determined by the interaction of land prices（土地价格）, construction costs（建设成本）, regulatory requirements（监管要求）, and demand for housing in a particular location. In successful cities with strong economies and growing populations, housing costs often rise faster than incomes, creating affordability challenges（可负担性挑战）that affect economic competitiveness（经济竞争力）, social equity（社会公平）, and quality of life.

Land（土地）in cities is a fundamentally scarce resource（根本稀缺的资源）. The supply of land in desirable urban locations — near employment centres, good schools（优质学校）, transport hubs（交通枢纽）, and amenities（便利设施）— is fixed or very limited, while demand is high and growing. This imbalance（失衡）drives up land prices and, consequently, housing costs. The price of urban land reflects the value of location（区位价值）— the access it provides to jobs, services, social networks, and opportunities. A small apartment（小公寓）in a central location may cost more than a large house in a peripheral area because the location provides greater access to economic and social opportunities.

Living costs（生活成本）in cities include housing, food, transport, utilities（公用事业费）, childcare（儿童保育）, and other expenses. Cities generally have higher living costs than rural areas, primarily driven by housing costs. Cities also offer higher wages, which can offset higher costs for people with in-demand skills and stable employment. For lower-income workers（低收入工人）, service workers（服务业工人）, and people in precarious employment（不稳定就业者）, high living costs can consume a disproportionate share of income（收入中不成比例的份额）, leaving little for savings（储蓄）, education, healthcare, or investment in the future.

Housing affordability（住房可负担性）is commonly measured by the ratio of housing costs to household income（住房成本与家庭收入之比）. Housing is generally considered affordable when it costs no more than about 30 percent of household income. In many major global cities（全球主要城市）— London（伦敦）, New York（纽约）, Sydney（悉尼）, Hong Kong, Vancouver（温哥华）— median housing costs（中位住房成本）far exceed this threshold, creating a housing affordability crisis（住房可负担性危机）that forces households to make difficult trade-offs between housing quality, location, and other essential expenditures.

Governments use various policies to address housing affordability, each targeting different parts of the supply-demand equation（供需等式）. Building public housing（公共住房建设）or social housing（社会住房）provides affordable options for low-income households directly. Housing subsidies（住房补贴）and housing vouchers（住房券）help low-income families afford market-rate housing（市场租金住房）. Inclusionary zoning（包容性分区）requires developers（开发商）to include affordable units（可负担住房单元）in new residential projects. Land-use reform（土地使用改革）— allowing higher density development（更高密度开发）, reducing parking requirements（减少停车要求）, streamlining approval processes（简化审批流程）— increases housing supply in high-demand areas, addressing the root cause of high prices. Rent stabilisation（租金稳定）policies limit how much landlords can increase rents, protecting existing tenants（现有租户）from displacement（流离失所）but potentially reducing incentives for new construction and maintenance.

Housing, land, and living costs therefore represent the mechanism through which urban land scarcity translates into affordability challenges and how policy responses attempt to address those challenges. The vocabulary of housing — housing affordability, land price, living cost, public housing, inclusionary zoning, land-use reform, rent stabilisation — names the factors that determine how much urban residents pay for housing and the policy tools that attempt to make housing accessible to all income levels. Urban texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from land scarcity through housing markets to the social outcomes that determine whether urban residents can afford to live near economic opportunities or whether they are pushed to the margins of the city.

## Transport, Commuting, and Mobility（交通、通勤与流动性）

Transport（交通）is the system that moves people and goods within and between urban areas. An efficient transport system allows people to access jobs, education, healthcare, and social activities; enables businesses to receive supplies（接收供应）and deliver products; and connects different parts of the city into a functioning economic and social whole. Transport is the circulatory system of a city（城市的循环系统）— when it functions well, the city thrives; when it fails, economic activity, social connection, and quality of life all suffer.

Commuting（通勤）is the regular travel between home and work or school. For many urban residents, commuting is a significant portion of daily life — the average commute time（平均通勤时间）varies greatly between cities, from less than 25 minutes in smaller cities to over 60 minutes in large metropolitan areas（大都市区）. Long commutes reduce personal time（个人时间）, increase stress（增加压力）, cost money for transport, reduce time available for family, exercise, and community participation, and contribute to air pollution and carbon emissions（碳排放）. Research consistently shows that long commutes are associated with lower life satisfaction（更低的生活满意度）, worse health outcomes（更差的健康结果）, and reduced social participation（减少的社会参与）.

Mobility（流动性）refers to the ability of people to move around the city and reach the destinations（目的地）they need and want to access. Good mobility means people can reach work, school, shops, healthcare, and social activities within a reasonable time and cost. Mobility is determined by the design of the transport system, the density and layout of the city（城市的密度和布局）, the availability of different transport options（不同交通选择的可获得性）, and the affordability of each option. Mobility is not merely about speed — it is about access（可及性）: a person living in a dense, mixed-use neighbourhood（密集混合用途社区）with good public transport may have better access to more destinations than a person living in a car-dependent suburb, even if the suburban resident drives at higher speeds.

Public transport（公共交通）— buses（公交车）, trains（火车）, subways（地铁）, trams（有轨电车）, light rail（轻轨）— is essential for mobility in dense cities. Public transport can move large numbers of people efficiently, using less road space（更少的道路空间）and producing less pollution per passenger-kilometre（每乘客公里污染）than private cars（私家车）. Cities with comprehensive, reliable, and affordable public transport systems have higher overall mobility, less congestion, lower per-capita transport emissions, and greater equity（更大的公平性）because public transport provides mobility to people who cannot drive — children, elderly people, people with disabilities, and low-income households.

Active transport（主动交通）— walking（步行）and cycling（骑行）— produces zero emissions, improves physical health, requires minimal infrastructure compared with motorised transport, and enhances the quality of urban environments. Many cities are investing in cycling infrastructure（自行车基础设施）— protected bike lanes（受保护的自行车道）, bike-sharing systems（共享单车系统）, secure parking（安全停车）— and pedestrian infrastructure（步行基础设施）— wider sidewalks（更宽的人行道）, pedestrian zones（步行区）, safe crossings（安全过街设施）— to encourage active transport and reduce car dependence（减少汽车依赖）. The "15-minute city"（15分钟城市）concept envisions urban neighbourhoods where all daily needs — work, shopping, education, healthcare, recreation — can be met within a 15-minute walk or bike ride, reducing the need for motorised transport entirely.

Transport, commuting, and mobility therefore represent the mechanism through which people move around cities and how transport systems determine whether urban residents can access economic opportunities and social services. The vocabulary of transport — commuting, mobility, public transport, active transport, 15-minute city, car dependence — names the systems through which people navigate urban space and the design choices that determine whether cities are accessible to all residents or only to those who can afford private vehicles. Urban texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from transport system design through mobility outcomes to the social outcomes that determine whether urban residents can participate fully in city life or whether transport barriers isolate them from economic and social opportunities.

## Infrastructure and Public Services（基础设施与公共服务）

Infrastructure（基础设施）is the physical systems（物理系统）that support urban life and economic activity: water supply networks（供水网络）, sewage and waste treatment（污水和废物处理）, electricity grids（电网）, gas distribution（燃气配送）, telecommunications（电信）, roads, bridges, tunnels（隧道）, public transport systems, and public buildings（公共建筑）. Infrastructure is the foundation（基础）that makes urban life possible — without functioning infrastructure, cities cannot operate regardless of how well-planned or well-governed they are in other respects.

Public services（公共服务）are services provided or organised by government to residents: education（教育）, healthcare（医疗保健）, police and fire services（警察和消防服务）, waste collection（垃圾收集）, parks and recreation（公园和娱乐）, libraries（图书馆）, and social services（社会服务）. The quality, accessibility, and reliability of public services strongly affect quality of life（生活质量）, property values（房产价值）, economic competitiveness, and social equity. Well-delivered public services make cities liveable（宜居的）; poorly delivered or inaccessible services create inequality, frustration, and social tension.

Infrastructure requires significant investment（大量投资）to build, maintain, and upgrade over its operational lifetime. Roads need periodic resurfacing（定期重新铺装）, water pipes need replacement（更换）before they burst（爆裂）, public transport systems need capacity expansion（容量扩展）as populations grow, and electrical grids need modernisation（现代化）to accommodate renewable energy（可再生能源）and electric vehicles（电动汽车）. When infrastructure is neglected（被忽视）, it deteriorates（恶化）and eventually fails — sometimes gradually through declining service quality, sometimes catastrophically（灾难性地）through bridge collapses（桥梁坍塌）, water main breaks（水管破裂）, or power grid failures（电网故障）. Many older cities in developed countries face the challenge of aging infrastructure（老化基础设施）built decades ago that needs replacement or major rehabilitation（大规模修复）at enormous cost.

The demand for infrastructure grows with urbanisation and population growth（人口增长）. New residents need housing, water, electricity, transport, schools, and healthcare facilities. When infrastructure investment（基础设施投资）does not keep pace with population growth, existing systems become overstretched（过度拉伸）, service quality declines, and the city becomes less liveable and less economically competitive. Infrastructure planning（基础设施规划）involves decisions about what to build, where to build it, when to build it, and how to pay for it. Good planning considers future population projections（未来人口预测）, changing technology（变化中的技术）, environmental impacts（环境影响）, climate resilience（气候韧性）, and the needs of different communities — including those that have historically been underserved（历史上服务不足的社区）.

Infrastructure and public services therefore represent the mechanism through which cities provide the physical systems and services that make urban life possible. The vocabulary of infrastructure — infrastructure, public service, infrastructure investment, infrastructure planning, aging infrastructure, climate resilience — names the physical systems that support urban life and the planning decisions that determine whether those systems can meet the needs of growing populations. Urban texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from infrastructure investment through service delivery to the urban outcomes that determine whether cities can function effectively or whether infrastructure failure degrades quality of life and economic competitiveness.

## Pollution, Green Space, and Liveability（污染、绿地与宜居性）

Pollution（污染）is a major environmental and public health problem in many cities, arising from the concentration of people, vehicles, industries, and energy consumption in limited space. Air pollution（空气污染）comes primarily from vehicle emissions（车辆排放）, industrial activity（工业活动）, construction dust（建筑扬尘）, and heating buildings（建筑供暖）. Water pollution（水污染）results from inadequate sewage treatment（污水处理不足）, industrial discharge（工业排放）, and stormwater runoff（雨水径流）carrying pollutants from urban surfaces. Noise pollution（噪音污染）from traffic, construction, and industrial activity affects millions of urban residents, contributing to stress, sleep disturbance（睡眠障碍）, and cardiovascular disease.

Air pollution has serious and well-documented health effects（有据可查的健康影响）. Fine particulate matter（细颗粒物 / PM2.5）from vehicle exhaust（车辆尾气）, industrial emissions, and combustion processes（燃烧过程）can penetrate deep into the lungs（深入肺部）and enter the bloodstream（进入血液）, causing respiratory diseases（呼吸系统疾病）, cardiovascular diseases（心血管疾病）, stroke（中风）, lung cancer（肺癌）, and adverse pregnancy outcomes（不良妊娠结果）. The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes approximately seven million premature deaths（过早死亡）worldwide each year, with the highest burden（最高负担）in rapidly industrialising cities in Asia and Africa. Children（儿童）, elderly people（老年人）, and people with pre-existing conditions（已有疾病者）are most vulnerable.

Green space（绿地）— parks, gardens, urban forests（城市森林）, green corridors（绿色廊道）, and natural areas within cities — provides multiple benefits that improve urban environmental quality and human wellbeing. Green spaces improve air quality（改善空气质量）by absorbing pollutants（吸收污染物）and producing oxygen. They reduce the urban heat island effect（城市热岛效应）by providing shade（遮荫）and cooling through evapotranspiration（蒸散作用）. They absorb stormwater（吸收雨水）, reducing flood risk（降低洪水风险）and relieving pressure on drainage systems. They provide opportunities for recreation（娱乐）, exercise（锻炼）, social interaction, and contact with nature（接触自然）— all of which improve physical and mental health. Access to green space has been consistently linked to better mental health（更好的心理健康）, lower stress levels（更低的压力水平）, reduced depression（减少抑郁）, and improved cognitive function（改善认知功能）, particularly among children and elderly people.

Liveability（宜居性）refers to the overall quality of life in a city, encompassing（包含）the physical, social, economic, and environmental conditions that determine how pleasant, healthy, safe, and fulfilling（充实的）it is to live there. Liveable cities are safe, clean, green, well-served by transport and public services, and offer diverse housing options, economic opportunities, and cultural amenities（文化设施）. Liveability is influenced by air quality, access to green space, transport efficiency and affordability, housing costs, crime rates（犯罪率）, quality of public services, social cohesion（社会凝聚力）, cultural vibrancy（文化活力）, and governance quality（治理质量）. Liveability rankings（宜居性排名）produced by organisations such as the Economist Intelligence Unit（经济学人智库）and Mercer（美世）assess cities across these dimensions and influence where skilled workers（技术工人）, businesses, and investment choose to locate.

Pollution, green space, and liveability therefore represent the mechanism through which urban environmental quality affects human health and the overall quality of urban life. The vocabulary of liveability — pollution, green space, air quality, urban heat island effect, liveability, social cohesion — names the environmental conditions that determine whether cities are healthy places to live and the urban design choices that can improve or degrade those conditions. Urban texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from urban pollution through environmental quality to the health and wellbeing outcomes that determine whether cities attract or repel residents, businesses, and investment.

## Sustainable Cities and Urban Planning（可持续城市与城市规划）

Sustainable cities（可持续城市）meet the needs of current residents without compromising the ability of future generations（后代）to meet their own needs. Sustainability in cities involves balancing economic development（经济发展）, social equity（社会公平）, and environmental protection（环境保护）— the three pillars of sustainable development（可持续发展的三大支柱）. A sustainable city uses resources efficiently（高效使用资源）, minimises waste and pollution（最小化浪费和污染）, protects natural ecosystems（保护自然生态系统）, provides equitable access to opportunities and services（公平获取机会和服务）, and builds resilience to climate change and other shocks（对气候变化和其他冲击的韧性）.

Urban planning（城市规划）is the process of designing and managing the physical development（物理发展）of cities — how land is used（土地使用方式）, how people move（人们如何移动）, where housing is built（住房建在哪里）, how infrastructure is provided（基础设施如何提供）, and how the natural environment is protected（自然环境如何保护）. Planning decisions made today shape cities for decades or centuries — the street layout（街道布局）, building density（建筑密度）, transport networks（交通网络）, and green spaces established by planners determine the daily experience of generations of residents. Good urban planning anticipates future needs（预见未来需求）, considers long-term consequences（考虑长期后果）, and balances competing interests（平衡竞争性利益）through evidence-based analysis（基于证据的分析）and inclusive public participation（包容性公众参与）.

Key principles of sustainable urban planning include several interrelated approaches. Compact development（紧凑发展）builds at higher densities to reduce urban sprawl（城市蔓延）, preserve surrounding natural areas and agricultural land（保护周边自然区域和农业用地）, and make public transport and services more efficient. Mixed-use development（混合用途开发）combines residential, commercial, office, and recreational uses in the same neighbourhood, reducing the need for long trips（减少长途出行需求）and creating vibrant, walkable communities（充满活力、可步行的社区）. Transit-oriented development（公交导向开发 / TOD）concentrates higher-density development around public transport stations（公共交通站点）to encourage public transport use and reduce car dependence. Green infrastructure（绿色基础设施）— urban forests, green roofs（绿色屋顶）, permeable surfaces（透水表面）, bioswales（生物洼地）— manages stormwater, reduces heat, improves air quality, and enhances biodiversity（增强生物多样性）within the urban fabric（城市肌理）.

Green buildings（绿色建筑）are designed and constructed to use less energy, water, and materials than conventional buildings while providing healthier indoor environments（更健康的室内环境）. They incorporate energy-efficient design（节能设计）— insulation（隔热）, natural ventilation（自然通风）, efficient lighting and appliances（高效照明和电器）— renewable energy generation（可再生能源发电）such as rooftop solar panels（屋顶太阳能板）, water-saving fixtures（节水装置）, sustainable building materials（可持续建筑材料）, and waste reduction strategies（废物减少策略）. Green building certification systems（绿色建筑认证体系）such as LEED and BREEAM provide standards and incentives for sustainable construction（可持续建设）.

Cities are also adapting to climate change（适应气候变化）through resilience planning（韧性规划）. Coastal cities（沿海城市）are building sea walls（海堤）, elevating infrastructure（抬升基础设施）, and developing managed retreat strategies（有序撤退策略）for areas that cannot be protected. Cities in hot regions（炎热地区）are planting urban forests, installing cool roofs（冷屋顶）and reflective surfaces（反射表面）, and developing heat action plans（高温行动方案）to protect vulnerable populations. Cities in flood-prone areas（洪水易发地区）are improving drainage, creating floodable parks（可淹没公园）, and restricting development in floodplains（洪泛区）. Urban planning that integrates climate adaptation（气候适应）with sustainable development creates cities that are both environmentally responsible（环境负责的）and resilient to the challenges of the coming decades.

Sustainable cities and urban planning therefore represent the mechanism through which cities attempt to balance economic development, social equity, and environmental protection. The vocabulary of sustainable cities — sustainable city, urban planning, compact development, mixed-use development, transit-oriented development, green infrastructure, green building, climate adaptation — names the design principles and planning approaches that determine whether cities can meet the needs of current residents without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Urban texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from planning decisions through urban design to the long-term outcomes that determine whether cities can provide opportunity, wellbeing, and sustainability for their growing populations.
